  3. Writing Wren's JavaScript glue in Odin

#Writing Wren's JavaScript glue in Odin

Wren's JavaScript engine is QuickJS-ng compiled to one WebAssembly module (build/js/wren_js.wasm). Around the engine sits the glue: the code that implements the web platform's objects and functions as QuickJS native functions and wires them to the browser's wr_* imports. Today most of that glue is hand-written C (native/js/runtime/*.c, ~47 000 lines) plus generated C (native/js/gen, bindgen). The goal is to move it to Odin, keeping only the Rust libraries and the upstream QuickJS C.

This document is the recipe. It is backed by two proofs in the tree:

  • native/js/odin_spike/ — the minimal link proof (Odin ↔ C ↔ JS in one module), run by src/tools/spiketest.
  • native/js/odin/ — the real glue layer (wj) and the first ported domain (web_strategy.odin), linked into the production engine by tools/build_js.ps1 and exercised through build/jsengine.exe.

#What was proven

  • An Odin procedure compiled to a wasm32 object links, with zig's wasm-ld, into the same module as the QuickJS objects that zig cc produces. It calls the QuickJS C API, is called from JavaScript as a native function, and C can call it directly. The reverse (C → Odin) works too.
  • CountQueuingStrategy / ByteLengthQueuingStrategy (the Streams Standard queuing strategies) were ported from native/js/runtime/web_strategy.c to native/js/odin/web_strategy.odin with identical behaviour; the C file is dropped from the build and the generated binding table resolves to the Odin wjr_* functions unchanged.

#The ABI: JSValue is a u64

The single most important fact. On wasm32 (INTPTR_MAX < INT64_MAX), QuickJS-ng turns on NAN boxing (quickjs.h: #define JS_NAN_BOXING 1, then typedef uint64_t JSValue). So a JSValue is a bare 64-bit integer, and every glue function passes and returns it in a single wasm i64. There is no struct-by-value ABI question on this target: Odin's u64 matches C's JSValue exactly, by value, in parameters and results.

The native-function signature (JSCFunction) is therefore, in Odin:

Odin
proc "c" (ctx: ^wj.Context, this_val: wj.JSValue, argc: i32, argv: [^]wj.JSValue) -> wj.JSValue

which is byte-for-byte the C JSValue (*)(JSContext *, JSValueConst, int, JSValueConst *). Getters and setters drop the argc/argv the obvious way (wj.Getter, wj.Setter).

#Three kinds of symbol

When wasm-ld links the Odin object with the C objects, a name either resolves to a C definition in the module, or it does not and becomes an import from env (which then traps at run time). So the glue layer must know, for each engine function it uses, whether that function has a real symbol.

  1. Real symbols — functions declared JS_EXTERN in quickjs.h, and the wj_* / web_* functions of native/js/engine and native/js/runtime. Declare them in an Odin foreign block with the exact C name and signature; wasm-ld resolves them to the C definitions. Examples: JS_GetPropertyStr, JS_ToFloat64, JS_NewNumber, JS_ThrowTypeError, wj_new_object, web_this_impl, web_dict_get.
  1. static inline helpers and macros — the value constructors and predicates of quickjs.h/qjs_backend.h (JS_NewInt32, JS_IsException, the JS_UNDEFINED constant, wj_arg…). These have no symbol; a foreign declaration of them would become an unresolved import. Reimplement them in Odin. With NAN boxing they are a few bit operations — see new_int32, is_exception, arg in native/js/odin/wj/wj.odin.
  1. Fields of C global structs — e.g. wj_the_realm.global. A struct field has no symbol either, and mirroring the wj_realm layout in Odin is fragile. Until wj_the_realm itself is ported, expose what you need through one tiny C accessor (native/js/odin/wj_shim.c: wj_realm_global()). This shim is only an accessor; it holds no logic and shrinks as more of the engine moves to Odin.

#Pitfall: reimplementing the NAN-box float encoding

JS_NewInt32 is trivial ((u64(tag) << 32) | u32(val)) and reimplementing it in Odin works. The float constructor __JS_NewFloat64 is bits(d) - (ADDEND << 32) with u64 wraparound — and the Odin build miscomputed that 64-bit wrapping subtraction for ordinary operands (a 3.5 came back as NaN). Do not reimplement the float encoding. Use the engine's real JS_NewNumber(ctx, d) symbol instead (that is why wj.new_float64 takes a ctx, unlike the inline C version). It also chooses the int representation for integral doubles exactly as the engine expects. The lesson generalises: when a real symbol exists, prefer it over reproducing the engine's internal bit tricks.

#The wj helper layer (native/js/odin/wj/wj.odin)

This is the Odin equivalent of engine/wj.h + qjs_backend.h + the parts of runtime/web.h a ported domain uses. It is the artifact other agents build on. It provides:

  • Types: JSValue (u64), Context/Runtime (opaque), Native/Getter/Setter (the function signatures).
  • Value constructors/predicates (inline, NAN-box): new_bool, new_int32, new_float64 (via JS_NewNumber), is_exception/undefined/null/object/string/number, the UNDEFINED/NULL/EXCEPTION/TRUE/FALSE constants, arg.
  • Engine functions (real symbols) in foreign blocks: JS_GetPropertyStr, JS_SetPrototype, JS_FreeValue, JS_DupValue, JS_ToFloat64, JS_ToInt32, JS_IsFunction, JS_ThrowTypeError (C varargs via #c_vararg), JS_ThrowOutOfMemory, JS_NewCFunction2 (+ the inline new_cfunction), JS_GetGlobalObject, JS_NewNumber.
  • wj.h helpers: wj_new_object, wj_malloc/wj_free (aliased malloc/free), and iface(name) which resolves an interface index by name through wj_interface_find (so the glue never hardcodes the generated WJ_IFACE_* numbers and survives their renumbering).
  • web.h helpers a domain needs: web_this_impl, web_dict_check, web_dict_get, web_extra_get, web_extra_set, and realm_global() (through the shim).

Grow this layer as you port domains: add the foreign declarations and inline helpers the new domain needs, keeping names and signatures matched to the C.

#Writing a domain (worked example)

See native/js/odin/web_strategy.odin. The rules:

  • The package is odin_glue (one package for all ported domains, so they share one object).
  • Every function the generated binding table references keeps its exact C name via @(export, link_name = "wjr_<Interface>_<member>"). The table in native/js/gen/bindings.c is unchanged; wasm-ld resolves its forward references to your Odin exports.
  • The signatures are proc "c" with the wj types.
  • Engine-owned object data (the C impl) is allocated with wj.malloc, stored with wj.wj_new_object(ctx, iface, impl, free_proc), and read back with wj.web_this_impl(ctx, this, iface). The free_proc is a proc "c" (p: rawptr) that calls wj.free.
  • Resolve interface indices once, by name, and cache them (see count_iface / bytelen_iface).

#Building

tools/build_js.ps1 was taught to include the Odin glue:

  • native/js/odin/*.odin → one wasm32 object (odin build -build-mode:obj -target:freestanding_wasm32 -no-entry-point -default-to-nil-allocator -o:size).
  • native/js/odin/wj_shim.c is compiled with the rest of the C.
  • A $odinified list names the C files that have been ported; they are dropped from the C sources. Today: web_strategy.c.
  • Linking: the C is compiled to plain wasm objects (no -flto) and linked with the Odin object without LTO. Why: Odin's freestanding wasm runtime defines memset/memcpy/memmove/bzero as strong symbols (it assumes no libc), and so does wasi-libc. A one-shot LTO link rejects the duplicate as a hard error; a plain-object link only warns (the definitions are semantically identical). So the build drops cross-TU LTO while an Odin object is present.

#The LTO trade-off (known, measured)

  • Dropping cross-TU LTO is the one real cost. In this spike it did not grow the module (the pre-initialized wren_js.wasm was smaller without LTO — 3901 KiB vs 5060 KiB — because LTO's aggressive inlining expands the memory image the snapshot captures). The runtime effect of losing LTO was not benchmarked here and is the lead's call.
  • A bonus: per-TU compilation makes incremental engine builds much faster (zig caches unchanged objects: ~3 s to rebuild after a one-file change, vs ~32 s for the one-shot LTO build that recompiled everything).
  • Paths to reclaim LTO later, if wanted: (a) stop Odin emitting the libc memory functions (needs an Odin option or a patched base:runtime); (b) do the final link with wasm-ld directly, placing the Odin object before libc.a so the libc members are never pulled (needs reproducing zig's sysroot link line); (c) weaken the Odin object's four memory symbols with llvm-objcopy before linking. None were needed to make the glue work.

#Reproduce

PowerShell
# the minimal link proof
powershell -NoProfile -File native\js\odin_spike\build_spike.ps1
odin build src\tools\spiketest -collection:wb=src -vet -out:build\spike\spiketest.exe -o:speed -extra-linker-flags:/STACK:33554432
build\spike\spiketest.exe build\spike\spike.wasm        # "spike: all checks passed"

# the engine with the Odin-ported domain
powershell -NoProfile -File tools\build_js.ps1
build\jsengine.exe run -e "var c = new CountQueuingStrategy({highWaterMark: 7}); console.log(c.highWaterMark, c.size(0))"
#   -> 7 1
